pack.title: A charge inventory for four laboratory samples

provenance.notes: Written for the exam-alignment pass of 22 November 2026, against topics reported first-hand from the 26 September 2026 sitting. Original scenario, original figures, no official topic reused. Automated gates only — not yet read by a person.

blocks.text: Counting charge in the Halden detector

Three kinds of particle make up the samples in this study. A proton carries one unit of positive charge. An electron carries one unit of negative charge. A neutron carries no charge at all. The net charge of a sample is the number of protons it contains minus the number of electrons it contains, counted in those same units, and neutrons never enter that calculation.

The detector counts each kind of particle separately and reports the totals. A sample holding exactly as many electrons as protons is called neutral. A sample holding more electrons than protons has taken on extra electrons, and one holding fewer has lost some; the number taken on or lost is the size of the difference between the two counts.

questions.stem: What is the net charge of sample S1, in the units used by the study?

supportSpans.quote: the number of protons it contains minus the number of electrons it contains

questions.explanation: S1 holds 26 protons and 24 electrons. The net charge is the proton count minus the electron count, which is 26 minus 24, or plus 2 units. The 30 neutrons are ignored, because the source states that neutrons never enter the calculation.

opt-b.reason: This subtracts the protons from the electrons instead. The source fixes the order: protons first, then electrons taken away from them.

opt-c.reason: This adds the neutron count into the total. The source states explicitly that neutrons carry no charge and never enter the calculation.

opt-d.reason: This adds the protons and electrons together rather than subtracting. Adding them would treat an electron as adding charge, when it carries the opposite sign to a proton.

hints.text: Only two of the four columns in the table matter for this question. The paragraph says which.
The two particles that carry charge carry it in opposite senses, so one count is taken away from the other.
Read the order of the subtraction off the source rather than choosing it, because reversing it flips the sign of the answer.

questions.stem: Which sample has taken on the greatest number of extra electrons?

supportSpans.quote: A sample holding more electrons than protons has taken on extra electrons

questions.explanation: A sample has taken on extra electrons when it holds more electrons than protons, and the number taken on is the size of that difference. S4 holds 10 electrons against 8 protons, a difference of two. S2 holds 18 against 17, a difference of one. S1 holds fewer electrons than protons and S3 holds equal numbers, so neither has taken any on. S4 therefore has the greatest number.

opt-b.reason: S2 has indeed taken on extra electrons, but only one of them. Another sample in the table has a larger excess of electrons over protons.

opt-c.reason: S1 holds fewer electrons than protons, so by the definition in the source it has lost electrons rather than taken any on.

opt-d.reason: S3 holds exactly as many electrons as protons, which the source calls neutral. A neutral sample has taken on none.

hints.text: The question is about a comparison between two columns, done once for each row of the table.
Work out the difference between the electron count and the proton count for every sample before choosing.
A difference in the other direction does not count here, and neither does a difference of zero.
